title: Leaderboard v2: two parts merged into one design
caption: Part "rank reads" adds the sorted set; part "score ingest" adds the queue and worker. They share the API node.

steps.text: Write path: store the best score durably first, then publish an event. The player gets 200 right away.
The updater applies events to an in-memory sorted set. Ranks lag by seconds, which the requirements allow.
Read path: rank and top-n come from the sorted set in O(log n), well under 100 ms.
Failure plan: lose the sorted set and you rebuild it from the scores DB, which stays the source of truth.

scenarios.name: Sorted set lost
scenarios.summary: The cache node holding the sorted set dies: reads fall back to the DB for top-n, and the worker rebuilds the set from the source of truth.

steps.text: The cache node restarts and the in-memory sorted set is gone.
Writes still succeed: the best score is in the DB and the event is queued.
Reads degrade: top-100 comes from the DB index; "my rank" returns "updating" for a few minutes.
The updater reloads all scores from the DB and replays the queue; ranks are back. A replica of the set would make this seconds.

scenarios.name: Tournament burst
scenarios.summary: At the end of a tournament writes jump 20×: the queue absorbs the burst, so the API stays fast while ranks lag for a little longer.

steps.text: Everyone submits a final score in the same minute: ~12 000 writes/s instead of 600.
The API upserts and publishes; the queue grows instead of the API slowing down.
The updater drains at its own pace: ranks lag by a minute instead of seconds, which the requirements tolerate.
Alert on queue lag, and add updater workers (partitioned by board) if it keeps growing.

scenarios.name: Alternative: dual write
scenarios.summary: Write to the DB and the sorted set in the request itself: two fewer boxes and fresh ranks, but a failed second write leaves the stores out of sync.

steps.text: A score arrives. The API upserts it in the DB, then ZADDs it to the sorted set, before answering.
Ranks are fresh immediately and there is no queue or worker to run.
But if the ZADD fails after the DB write, the stores disagree until a repair job runs; and the write latency includes both stores.
Fine at 600 writes/s with a nightly reconcile; the queue version wins once bursts or strict durability matter.
